questions.explain: Databases are stateful — tests can interfere with each other or leave residue — and many database changes (drop column, truncate, partition migration) are effectively irreversible, making a failed database deployment far costlier than a bad application build.
options: The database is stateful and changes are often irreversible in practice, so a failed database deployment costs far more than rolling back an application build.
Database tests require more servers than application tests.
SQL Server cannot run tests in transactions.
Application tests never touch the database.
questions.q: Why is database testing fundamentally different from application testing, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: The relevant dimensions are data volume, data distribution, schema version, configuration settings (e.g., MAXDOP, cost threshold), and hardware/resources. Restoring a backup with a new name (WITH MOVE) or using snapshots/BACPAC are the typical SQL Server approaches — and masked data should preserve realistic cardinality so plans stay representative.
options: Same SQL Server version only — data volume does not matter.
Data volume, schema version, configuration settings (e.g., MAXDOP, cost threshold), and resources — a 10,000-row staging database cannot predict plans on 80 million rows.
Only the hardware matters; everything else is cosmetic.
Only the database name must match production.
questions.q: Which dimensions of a test environment must mirror production for test results to be meaningful?

questions.explain: Before adding NOT NULL, check for nulls; before a unique constraint, identify duplicates with GROUP BY/HAVING; before altering a column, check dependents with sys.dm_sql_referencing_entities. These pre-migration checks catch violations before they become deployment errors.
options: Whether the DBA has sysadmin rights.

Whether there are rows that would violate the new constraint, duplicate keys that would break a unique constraint, and dependent objects (via sys.dm_sql_referencing_entities) that the change would affect.
Whether the backup job succeeded last night.
Whether the application uses an ORM.
questions.q: Before applying a schema migration, what should the pre-migration checks cover?

questions.explain: Adding a FK validates existing rows by default; WITH NOCHECK adds it quickly as untrusted but the optimizer ignores untrusted constraints. Post-migration checks must verify trust status in sys.foreign_keys (is_not_trusted = 1) and validate later with WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT.
options: Untrusted constraints are automatically trusted after the next backup.
A foreign key added WITH NOCHECK is untrusted and ignored by the optimizer until validated — verify is_not_trusted in sys.foreign_keys and validate with WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT.
WITH NOCHECK has no effect on foreign keys, only on check constraints.
Untrusted constraints cause the restore sequence to fail.
questions.q: A migration adds a foreign key WITH NOCHECK for speed. Why must post-migration verification check sys.foreign_keys for is_not_trusted?

questions.explain: Reconciliation runs coarse-to-fine: total row count catches bulk failures, aggregates (sums, distinct counts, min/max) catch transformation bugs, then hash/checksum or EXCEPT-based row-by-row diffs catch subtle value discrepancies like encoding or whitespace issues.
options: Run EXCEPT on every row first, then check counts.
Row counts first, then aggregate checks (sums, distinct counts, min/max), then hash-based or EXCEPT row-level diffs — from coarse to fine.
Compare only the schema; row data is assumed correct if counts match.
Restore production over the target and skip validation.
questions.q: What is the correct order for data-migration reconciliation checks, and why?
